Gaussian Splatting # Gaussian splatting is a 3D digital reconstruction and rendering technique that uses millions of tiny, soft, overlapping 3D shapes called Gaussians to recreate real-world scenes with photorealistic detail and real-time viewing speeds. Here we use a database of photos to create make this reconstruction. We use Colmap, Brush and Supersplat to get the final result.
Colmap # First, we load the image database into Colmap, to detect features on each of them, and reconstruct them together to get the relations between each images
First visualisation of the object after detecting features and reconstructing Brush # Now, we use brush in order to train the database and perform the reconstruction, using Machine Learning. The app allows the user to see the rendering progress in real time.
Brush, training the database After the training, we can see that there are a lot of artifacts created, which we will try to remove to get a more polished look.
Final result from Brush Supersplat # To get our finished product, we use Supersplat to visualise the 3D object, as weell as remove any Gaussians that are not relevant to our
Final result after removing the irrelevant gaussians on Supersplat
Here is a interactive representation of the 3D object :
title: Gaussian Splatting

A current HCI research study # In this section, I will present the recent work of Weiwei He, who is working (together with other researchers) on a Biomimetic Flexible Sensor inspired by the natural layered structure of eggshells.This work was inspired by the great potential that biomimetic innovations have shown in recent years.
Their team designed the eggshell-inspired multifunctional hybrid flexible sensor (EMHFS), which uses 4 functional layers : a triboelectric layer for noncontact sensing, a piezoresistive layer for pressure sensing, and hydrophilic–hydrophobic layers for directional moisture wicking, breathability, and antibacterial properties.
This new flexible sensor can be useful for a variety of HCI scenarios, such as wearables, robotics or smart interactives devices.
Schematics from the research article illustrating the inspiration The Ultimate Display, by Ivan Sutherland # In this foreshadowing paper from 1965, Ivan Sutherland predicts how Human-Computer Interfaces could evolve in the future. Nowadays, we can see that his prediction where quite precise !
He predicted that computers will be interacted with using a keyboard (a “typewriter”), the apparition of drag-and-drop interfaces as well as voice inputs. He also conceptualized what became haptic feedbacks, where the user can feel resistance when interacting with an object.
Sutherland also describes technologies we don’t know of yet. The haptic feedbacks he imagined still isn’t as advanced today, so there is still room for improvement and many innovations could emerge in the upcomig years. His ultimate ambition is “a room within which the computer can control the existence of matter”. This still seems very far today, but maybe this could also become reality !
Ivan Sutherland and his head mounted display Input Device failing # Here I’ll talk about pre-touch sensing. This technology has been discussed more than 10 years ago (see the ACM SIGCHI video), but it has never gone mainstream. While they argue that it adds more depth to mobile interactions and is relatively easy and cheap to integrate to a device, the technology couldn’t find its way to our phones. This might be because pre-touch adds a new dimension to how we interact with our device, which it could also adds a way for the device to misinterpret the intention of the user. When the device detects the user approaching it, it might interpret it as them wanting to interact, but it might also be them just moving around. For this main reason, this technology didn’t get used much, prefering other ways to interact such as voice command, which is easier for the user to use while still completing complex tasks.
Pre-Touch Sensing for Mobile Interaction, by ACM SIGCHI on Youtube
title: Current research, the Ultimate Display & Input Devices

content:
Affordances # “An affordance is a relationship between the properties of an object and the capabilities of the agent that determine just how the object could possibly be used.” - Don Norman
A simple example of affordance would be cutlery. Their long shape naturally induce how it should held, as well as in which cases they should be used. For example a spoon’s curved bowl affords scooping and holding liquids, while a knife’s sharper shapes affords cutting.
A case of bad affordance is the mystery meat navigation. It is when a component of a web page is hidden until the user hovers his mouse on it. For example when articles are being refered to on Wikipédia, you can see a preview when hovering on their title. This is useful for a user on a computer, but it doesn’t work for a user on a smartphone. It would be difficult to solve this problem, but maybe it could be tackled by using a feature of the touchscreen. Something like a “zooming” motion could be a way to tell if the user wants to see the preview of an article.
Example of a preview when hovering on Wikipédia Gestalt Laws # Gestalt Laws is useful when tidying your computer desktop ! You can arrange the icons of the desktop however you want. I personaly like to keep related apps close to each others. This is an example of the law of Common-region, though this is not done automatically.
A classic Windows desktop Dark Design Patterns # Video games often use some dark patterns to either keep the players on the game, or even to get them to spend money. For example, the Daily Login Reward mechanic rewards the player for each consecutive day they log onto the game, making sure they open the app every day. A more sound approach to this would be to reward the user for playing regularly without imposing this daily login rule. The player could choose how often they intend to play the game, and still get a reward.
A login reward from a game Many websites use cookies and want their user to accept them. To do this, they use tactics to make it harder for the user to refuse them. It is mostly done through interface interference and obstruction, as the user can accept all cookies with a single click, but if they want to refuse them, several clicks are required. This would be simply fixed with a “reject all cookies” button, but it would require the website to be more honest and not want to trick the user in the first place.
Example of a cookie agreement pop-up
title: Affordances, Gestalt Law & Dark Design Patterns
